A diagnostic framework for interpreting spatiotemporal probabilistic forecasts
A review of optimization systems and methods for wastewater treatment plants operation
abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) play a critical role in managing sewage before it is released into the environment. As regulations become more stringent, plants must adapt to these changes, making the development of innovative methodologies for optimizing WWTPs essential. This work provides an overview of how WWTP operation optimization can be conducted. First, the fundamental aspects of WWTP processes, modelling, and operation are presented, along with the basics of optimization problems. This article then explores the application of WWTP operation optimization within the literature, starting with the formulation of the problem, followed by the methods used for optimization. The interaction between optimization systems and the plant, as well as their degree of implementation, is examined. Finally, the current developments and the existing gaps to obtain more complete and applicable optimization systems are discussed.

title: Flow in float: Memory-efficient upstream flow length parallel computation using an IEEE-754-based union encoding
Modelling the human impact on hydrological cycle: The MISDc v3.1 model
abstract: ABSTRACT This study presents MISDc v3.1 , a process-based, flexible and open-source hydrological model developed to simulate complex water dynamics in large and human-impacted river systems. The model is applied to the Po River basin, Italy, subjected to strong anthropogenic impact. Calibration uses hydrometeorological data from 2000–2023, while validation is performed through multi-variable comparison against observed river discharge and satellite-based measurements of soil moisture, evaporation, snow water equivalent, and irrigation volumes. Quantitative performance assessment indicates strong simulation accuracy across multiple gauge stations (modified Kling–Gupta Efficiency = 0.88–0.93). The inclusion of irrigation and reservoir operation modules markedly enhances river discharge simulations, particularly during low-flow conditions and the 2022–2023 extreme drought. Uncertainty, assessed through the BLUECAT method, fosters a better understanding of model reliability across flow regimes. Owing to its Python-based and open-access architecture, MISDc v3.1 is easily transferable to other basins, offering a robust and flexible tool for integrated water resources management.

title: Towards precision irrigation scheduling from UAV-based observations: Model structure
abstract: Precision irrigation scheduling is critical for improving agricultural water use. Root zone soil moisture (RZSM) governs crop water uptake and is therefore fundamental for precision irrigation. The effectiveness of RZSM estimation coupled with UAV-based observations depends on the model’s structural design and accuracy, and requires at least a two-layer representation, whereas soil moisture models for irrigation scheduling are often oversimplified single-layer buckets. To address this gap, a series of soil moisture models have been developed and tested, ranging from two- to multi-layer configurations with varying complexity, based on a conceptual bucket model framework. Key model components, including vertical soil moisture redistribution, evapotranspiration, drainage, and infiltration, were progressively refined and systematically evaluated. A two-layer model with soil moisture redistribution based on the Buckingham-Darcy equation and a water-stress adjusted evapotranspiration scheme (R-FLX-ET) was identified as the optimal configuration for achieving reliable soil moisture predictions with minimal complexity. The R-FLX-ET model achieved NSE values up to 0.92 for the root zone and 0.81 for the near-surface layer when applying an hourly resolution, with RMSE values below 0.03 cm³/cm³, outperforming the single-layer model (NSE=0.50 for hourly) and Aqua Crop (NSE=0.78 for daily RZSM estimations). Validation at four monitoring stations demonstrated the robustness of the R-FLX-ET model. Multi-layer extensions did not substantially improve the overall RZSM accuracy compared to the two-layer configuration. The performance of R-FLX-ET remained stable when the root zone depth varied between 15 cm and 60 cm, supporting its applicability to crops with diverse rooting systems. The R-FLX-ET model therefore provides a robust and computationally efficient framework that is also suited for integration with UAV-based near-surface soil moisture retrievals for enhanced RZSM mapping to support precision irrigation scheduling.

title: Improving precipitation forecasts through machine learning of the decomposed high- and low-frequency components
A novel coupled BN-PLUS-IC model for simulating land use change and carbon emissions under SSP-RCP scenarios: A case study of the Fujian Province, China
Estimation of lake storage volumes in the Lagan River catchment in southern Sweden using a modified version of the Australian Water Resources Assessment–Landscape model (AWRA-L)
abstract: In an era of global change, understanding available water resources is increasingly important. In Sweden, this challenge has intensified due to climate change driven pressures and rising water demand, yet suitable tools for assessing water storage remain limited. This study presents a novel approach for evaluating surface water storage using a modified Australian Water Resources Assessment Landscape model (AWRA-L). Physics-informed rating curves were incorporated during model optimization and tested over a five-year period (2018–2022) in a case study of three lakes in the Lagan River catchment, southwest Sweden. Results show that the modified model reproduces seasonal storage dynamics well, with average R 2 , NSE, and KGE′ values of 0.70, 0.68, and 0.71, respectively. Our findings suggest the approach has strong potential for accurately assessing surface storage dynamics and demonstrate that, with appropriate adaptation, the AWRA-L model is applicable outside Australia, offering an improved tool for evaluating lake storage volumes.

title: PyGREET: A modular Python platform of the GREET life cycle analysis model for technology assessment
abstract: The research and development version of the Greenhouse gases, Regulated Emissions, and Energy use in Technologies model (R&D GREET®) is a publicly available and widely-used model for life cycle analysis (LCA) of energy systems and emerging technologies. However, its Excel and .NET platforms face significant scaling and maintenance challenges. This paper introduces PyGREET, a modular Python-based platform designed for scalability and interoperability with other LCA tools like openLCA and Federal LCA Commons. PyGREET adopts a layered architecture to separate domain modeling from numerical solvers, facilitating maintenance, improving reusability for future web-hosted applications and R&D GREET derivatives. Validation against existing platforms confirms computational equivalence across technology pathways. By establishing a robust, modular software architecture, PyGREET enhances transparency, user experience, and interoperability. This platform provides a foundation for reliable LCA modeling and the continued annual expansion of R&D GREET at Argonne with advanced features for technology assessment and informed decision-making.

title: An integrated modeling platform for land-coast-ocean continuum: The Gulf of America coastal hazards forecast system (GAm-CHFS)
abstract: Highlights● The GAm-CHFS consists of 1) a Mississippi River Model (250m), 2) a GAm Ocean Model (1 km), and 3) several compound flooding models (100m).● The GAm-CHFS’s flexible model coupling, i.e., one-way river-ocean coupling and 2-way hydrological-ocean coupling, is crucial for flooding and water quality forecasts in coastal and ocean regions influenced by the Mississippi River● Developing a rapid and accurate AI model and ensemble forecasting system is prioritized for the GAm coastal hazards forecast.

title: Improving groundwater level prediction based on optimized deep learning model with Coati algorithm
Deep learning meets GPR: Exploring transformer models for precision soil depth prediction
Anomaly detection using continuous wavelet transforms and local active information storage scores: An application to water distribution networks
abstract: The identification of anomalies within time series is a mature field. This paper, however, introduces a distinct methodology tailored for detecting extremely subtle anomalies in data heavily corrupted by significant noise and trends originating from non-polynomial and nonlinear dynamics. Our innovative technique utilizes a tailored Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) based filtering pipeline to deconstruct data and effectively remove nonlinear and non-polynomial trends, subsequently leading to precise identification of anomalies using Local Active Information Storage (LAIS) as an unsupervised anomaly indicator. Our analysis of the LAIS scores makes it possible to detect anomalies. More specifically, this kind of analysis, when applied to steady pressures inside a Water Distribution Network (WDN), allows us to identify very tiny incipient leaks. We successfully tested our method on publicly available realistic synthetic data, pertaining to Hanoi WDN, containing minute leaks that other forefront methods available in literature were unable to detect.

title: From theory to practice. A shiny R app for climate-smart forestry assessment
abstract: Climate-Smart Forestry (CSF) integrates mitigation, adaptation, and socio-economic performance to address climate change in forest management. Despite the increasing use of CSF indicators, a standardized and user-friendly operational tool is still lacking. This study presents the Climate-Smart Forestry Assessment Tool (CSF-AT), a web-based application that automates the calculation of a composite climate-smart index, integrates the three CSF pillars, and generates visual outputs to support research and management decisions. The tool’s usability and versatility are demonstrated through two case studies. In the Collemeluccio Forest (Italy), CSF-AT highlights the climate-smartness implications of alternative silvicultural strategies and supports scenario exploration. A second application, using ICP Forests Level II data from Scots pine stands across five European countries, reveals spatial and temporal patterns and enables cross-country comparisons. Results confirm the tool’s applicability across scales, offering a transparent, standardized, and accessible platform that bridges the gap between CSF conceptual frameworks and its practical implementation.

title: Complexity vs. efficiency: Are full-structure Copula models worth the cost in multivariate hydrological simulation?
GIFIS: A generalized immersive flood information system specification
abstract: This study introduces Generalized Immersive Flood Information Specification (GIFIS), a vendor-agnostic, JSON Schema–based framework for encoding, validating, and exchanging hydrologic and environmental data for reproducible and interoperable virtual and augmented reality applications. By defining standardized semantics for entities such as sensor datasets, hydrological model outputs, warnings and alerts, and infrastructure assets, along with portable document types for spatial anchoring, scene composition, and evidence packaging, GIFIS transforms interoperability into a verifiable property of the data itself. A built-in validator enforces conformance through rule codes and machine-readable diagnostics, ensuring that information published once can be deterministically interpreted across analytical, operational, and immersive environments. Through its schema-centric and engine-neutral design, GIFIS enables any client to load and interpret hydrologic information without reliance on proprietary rendering pipelines or manual data harmonization for immersive platforms and applications. By coupling semantic rigor with open governance and extensibility, GIFIS establishes a sustainable foundation for transparent, FAIR-compliant flood information systems that bridge scientific research, operational decision support, and public communication.

title: Global structure-aware R-Tree: a spatial indexing mechanism using deep reinforcement learning and self-play
A hierarchical decision framework for low-cost sensor deployment in lake monitoring under uncertainty
Software tooling support for atmospheric dispersion modeling of the AERMOD system
abstract: Air pollution is a risk to public health. Identifying emission origins requires inventoried data to support air quality assessment. Then, simulations can be performed using the AERMOD system, recommended by the U.S. EPA. However, preparing the AERMOD input files is complex and error-prone because the data comes from multiple sources and must be in specific formats (e.g., SAM files). Since the available free tools have limitations and lack flexibility, users often rely on third-party services to obtain these files. This work presents AERMOD-IPT, an open-source tool that automates the generation of AERMOD input files. AERMOD-IPT was evaluated using BREEZEAERMOD/ISC and an emissions inventory from the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA) for 2019–2021 in Toledo, Paraná, Brazil, including particulate matter (PM 10 ), carbon monoxide (CO), and nitrogen oxides (NO x ). Results show high reliability, supported by contour-map agreement and a Kappa index (k > 0.97).

title: Quadratic decomposition and WOA-optimized CNN-ResNet-BiGRU-Attention: A novel hybrid framework for hydrological runoff forecasting
abstract: Accurate and reliable monthly runoff prediction is a crucial component of scientific water resources management. Due to the impacts of human activities and climate change, runoff series exhibit non-stationarity, which typically deteriorates the performance of most existing runoff prediction models. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel hydrological runoff forecasting model based on double decomposition and deep learning. The model first decomposes the runoff series using Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN). Then, the K-Means algorithm classifies the subsequences according to the sample entropy criterion and frequency characteristics. The Singular Spectrum Analysis-Variational Mode Decomposition (SSA-VMD) model is introduced to conduct a secondary decomposition of the high-frequency components. Subsequently, a CNN-ResNet-BiGRU model integrated with the Attention mechanism is optimized by the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) to simulate and predict the runoff series. The results of the monthly runoff series at the Longmen Hydrological Station in the Yellow River Basin demonstrate that the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) coefficient of the proposed model reaches 0.9743. Compared with the single VMD decomposition model, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the double decomposition model is reduced by 80.86%, and the NSE is increased by 18.27%. Moreover, simulation predictions at three hydrological stations in different regions of the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River Basin further verify the model's potential applicability, with all NSE values exceeding 0.95. This study provides an effective approach for monthly runoff prediction in non-stationary environments, which is of great significance for flood control and scientific water resources management.

title: A novel approach for retrieving water use efficiency and gross primary production from the “analytical triangle” technique: extending the Ts/VI feature space properties
abstract: Monitoring and quantifying the carbon-water exchange under climate change is a key indicator for the study of interactions between carbon and water cycles in terrestrial ecosystems. To support the growing need for monitoring surface–atmosphere exchange processes, the present study proposes a novel methodological framework for deriving carbon components from the Ts/VI feature space, coupled with land process-based modelling, which can be applied across local, regional, and large spatial scales using EO data. The current framework, introduces a proof-of-concept for a new scheme that extends the application of the “analytical” triangle, by producing spatially explicit, instantaneous maps of ambient gross primary productivity, carbon concentration, and water use efficiency. An initial evaluation of the proof-of-concept methodological framework was tested in 6 sites belong to the global network of ground measurements FLUXNET, across 5 different ecosystem types, for a total of 35 days, using the Landsat-8 EO data coupled with the SimSphere model. Results of GPP and WUE produced a small bias of -0.103 μmol CO 2 m −2 s −1 and RMSD of 7.66 μmol CO 2 m −2 s −1 and also a bias of 2.216 kg m −3 and RMSD of 4.54 kg m −3 , respectively. The predicted [CO 2 ] showed high deviation (bias of -18.24 μmol mol −1 ), and a moderate overall agreement (R = 0.52). The predictions have shown a reasonable level of agreement with FLUXNET observations, providing a preliminary proof of concept for the proposed method, with potential for future applications at regional to large scales. Yet, further investigation is ongoing to confirm its to access the method’s generality and its ability to represent physical processes across various ecosystems.

title: Composite2Change (C2C) on Google Earth Engine: Time-series change detection and metrics characterizing disturbance and recovery
abstract: Satellite time series enable the consistent and scalable characterization of land cover changes and vegetation dynamics across extensive areas. The Composite2Change (C2C) protocol applies temporal spectral trend analysis to identify land change events, producing metrics that describe the timing, magnitude, duration, rate, direction, and recovery dynamics of disturbances. These metrics summarize spectral trajectories and support mapping and modelling applications. While the methods have been published and their value demonstrated, their replication across regions and sensors has been limited due to high storage and computational demands, coupled with the lack of available implementation. To address these barriers, we implemented C2C as a reproducible cloud-native framework within Google Earth Engine (C2C-GEE). C2C-GEE enables users to generate change products and metrics that describe the spectral and temporal signatures of land cover change and recovery. The framework supports the transparent and systematic generation of standardized change metrics for large-area mapping and modelling applications worldwide.

title: Coupling process-based models with machine learning for the prediction of soil carbon and nitrogen cycling
Enhancing high-flow estimation in rainfall-runoff models using resampling techniques: applications to GR4J and Sacramento models
abstract: Floods cause significant damage globally, making accurate flood magnitude estimation crucial. However, limited high-flow observations can affect the skill of conceptual rainfall-runoff models for flood simulations. Data resampling techniques have shown improved model calibration for imbalanced datasets, but do not preserve the temporal structure of time series data needed to correctly represent flood behaviour in conceptual models. Here this issue is addressed by developing a modified Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) objective function incorporating resampling methods, specifically over-sampling (OS) and hybrid-sampling (HS). We calibrated the Genie Rural a 4 Parameters Journalier (GR4J) model and the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting Model (SAC) across 168 Australian catchments, focusing on flows exceeding the 99.8 th percentile. Compared to standard KGE and two high-flow objective functions (i.e., Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency with a penalty term and Annual Peak Flow Bias) our resampling-modified KGE improved high-flow estimation in most catchments, particularly those with lower baseflow indices and higher runoff skewness.

title: DarcyWarp: A graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated multigrid solver for repeated 2D fixed-transmissivity groundwater solves validated against reference solvers
abstract: Repeated steady-state groundwater solves for calibration and uncertainty analysis are often limited by runtime. We present DarcyWarp, a graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated geometric multigrid solver for two-dimensional, steady-state, single-layer groundwater flow using a fixed-transmissivity formulation on structured grids. DarcyWarp implements an explicit cell-integrated five-point finite-difference operator and multigrid cycle as Python kernels just in time compiled for GPU execution with NVIDIA Warp, and supports areal source/sink terms, prescribed head, no-flow, and general-head boundaries. Validation against a sparse finite-difference direct solve and MODFLOW 6 on matched grids shows close head agreement, consistent residuals, and mass-balance closure. Benchmarks span matched-grid single-instance cases from 1 0 4 to 9 × 1 0 6 active cells and two 48-case repeated-solve ensembles. DarcyWarp reaches about 70 times end-to-end speedup over MODFLOW 6 in the single-instance suite and order-of-magnitude throughput gains in ensembles, enabling reproducible repeated-solve workflows on commodity GPUs.

title: A graph-based approach for modeling landscape connectivity and analyzing runoff potential
abstract: We present an open-source Python pipeline to automate landscape modeling for hydrological analysis, addressing the limitations of manual GIS processing. The proposed reproducible GIS-to-graph workflow transforms geospatial land-use data into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to map functional connectivity. The core contribution integrates three sequential phases: data cleaning, structural consolidation of patch-boundary attributes, and topological generation. Nodes represent discrete soil patches, while directed edges represent topographic boundaries oriented by gravitational potential. The framework implements spatial graph algorithms—including degree centrality, Breadth-First Search, and an adapted Bellman-Ford procedure to identify potential runoff source areas and critical connectivity corridors within the model’s topological assumptions. Edges are weighted using a composite metric integrating elevation difference, land-cover contrast, and boundary length. A case study involving 1427 patches demonstrates high computational efficiency with O ( | V | + | E | ) complexity for path identification. This scalable software solution bridges computer science methodology and geoscientific applications, providing a robust tool for precision environmental management and runoff mitigation planning.

title: A tightly coupled socio-hydrological model with feedback pathways for water availability assessment: A case study of the Weihe River Basin
OpenEOcraft: A generic R-based framework for earth observation data cubes analysis
abstract: The openEO initiative provides a standardized interface for Earth Observation (EO) analytics, enabling workflows to be executed across different computational backends. Although openEO supports multiple client languages, integrating R-based analytical methods in cloud environments remains limited. Existing solutions, such as OpenEOcubes , offer partial support but do not provide a general mechanism for exposing the broader range of geospatial, statistical, and machine learning tools available in R as openEO processes. This paper presents OpenEOcraft , a framework that integrates R-based EO workflows into the openEO ecosystem through a three-layer design comprising an execution engine, a process translation layer, and a RESTful API. The framework allows analytical functions from established R libraries to be made available as openEO-compliant processes with limited development effort. Two use cases illustrate its capabilities: time-series-based land cover classification and machine learning model reuse supported by its metadata, both of which are reproducible across R, Python, and the openEO Web Editor. OpenEOcraft extends the range of R methods available in openEO and supports reproducible EO analytics across heterogeneous clients. • Brings R’s geospatial, geostatistical, and ML tools into the openEO ecosystem. • Modular three-layer design (engine, translator, REST API) for isolated R runtimes. • Decorator plugins: R functions tagged @openeo-process become processes. • openEO-conformant: reproducible, interoperable across R, Python, Julia clients. • Integrates STAC for interoperable, reproducible data access.

title: UQEF-Dynamic: A scalable open-source tool for forward uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis of time-varying model outputs
abstract: This work presents UQEF-Dynamic , an open-source Python tool for forward uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis of models with time-varying outputs, such as hydrological and environmental systems. Existing tools rarely handle high-dimensional, computationally expensive models with vectorial or functional outputs, nor do they fully exploit modern high-performance computing. UQEF-Dynamic addresses these gaps with a scalable, portable framework supporting sampling-based methods and non-intrusive Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE), extended with Karhunen–Loève (KL) surrogates to reduce output dimensionality, and enabling time-varying and generalized Sobol’ sensitivity indices. Alongside the software, this work provides a unified treatment of the underlying mathematical methods. We demonstrate the framework through two case studies: an analysis of the HBV-SASK hydrological model, to our knowledge the most comprehensive analysis of this model, and the construction of a KL–PCE surrogate for a 24-dimensional electrochemical battery model. Results show that UQEF-Dynamic delivers efficient analysis and deeper insight into model behavior under varying conditions.

title: Automating shoreline extraction from beach imaging systems for coastal monitoring
abstract: High-frequency coastal monitoring is essential for understanding shoreline dynamics under climate change and supporting coastal adaptation. Although ground-based remote sensing offers a scalable solution for data acquisition, automated shoreline extraction from beach imaging systems remains challenging due to variable image quality, complex geometries, and environmental conditions. This study presents a robust deep learning framework for instantaneous shoreline extraction from crowd-sourced imagery (i.e., smartphone captures). We benchmarked state-of-the-art segmentation models against a traditional histogram-based deterministic method. Results show that convolutional neural network approaches, particularly DeepLabV3 with 512 ×512 patches, significantly outperform conventional methods, achieving spatial reliability comparable to manual digitisation. Importantly, the model overcomes perspective distortion and interpolation artefacts in rectified imagery across diverse tidal environments, showing strong environmental robustness despite site diversity and data imbalance. The framework has been deployed as an open-source, containerised module within the European Open Science Cloud, enabling transferable and operational image-based coastline monitoring.

title: Coupling SWAT+ with machine learning-enhanced ECMWF seasonal forecasts for predicting inflows to Entrepeñas and Buendía reservoirs
abstract: ABSTRACT The Segura River Basin in southeastern Spain relies on the Tagus–Segura water transfer for agricultural activities. Reliable one- to three-month and seasonal reservoir inflow forecasts are essential for managing transfers from the Upper Tagus River Basin reservoirs (Entrepeñas and Buendía). This study develops a seasonal hydrological forecasting framework using ECMWF’s SEAS5 ensemble climate predictions. Bias-corrected forecasts with machine learning generate daily precipitation and temperatures up to seven months ahead. These drive a calibrated SWAT+ model to simulate reservoir inflows. Model calibration (2000-2009) and validation (2010-2019) showed strong performance (NSE > 0.7, PBIAS < 14%). Bias-corrected forecasts enabled skilful inflow predictions, with high reliability at 1–3 months (NSE = 0.91–0.73) and seasonal scales. Performance declines toward 7 months (NSE = 0.58), although CRPSS remains generally positive, outperforming traditional estimates calculated from historical data. This demonstrates the value of integrating seasonal climate forecasts into operational water-resource decision-making in drought-prone basins.

title: Geostatistical active learning for expanding monitoring networks for environmental decision-making: The case of groundwater nitrate
abstract: Expanding environmental monitoring networks is a spatial sampling problem often addressed with pointwise uncertainty heuristics that ignore the neighbourhood impact of new sites and the decision tasks motivating monitoring. We recast network densification as active learning and propose model-agnostic acquisition criteria, including a decision-aligned focal logit utility that prioritises neighbourhoods whose exceedance probabilities lie near regulatory thresholds. A look-ahead criterion based on the expected drop in prediction standard error (SE) is also examined. In a groundwater nitrate case study, the focal logit criterion consistently selected more informative sites than dispersion or SE heuristics, yielding up to 58% greater gains in exceedance-mapping accuracy (Cohen’s κ). Focal logit and SE criteria outperformed pointwise counterparts by ~45% on average, while the look-ahead criterion performed well at much higher computational cost. The framework is simple, generalisable to other pollutants, and supports transparent, decision-oriented monitoring design.

title: HydroBlox: AI-assisted visual programming framework for enhanced scientific reproducibility in hydrology
abstract: Scientific workflow reproducibility for hydrological and environmental analyses remains a challenge due to the heterogeneity of data sources, analysis protocols, and evolving visualization needs. This study introduces HydroBlox, a client-side browser-based framework that supports the creation, execution, and export of hydrological workflows using a visual programming interface. The platform integrates modular web libraries to perform data retrieval, statistical analysis, and visualization directly in the browser. Two case studies are presented to demonstrate the platform: precipitation–streamflow response analysis in the Iowa River Basin and SPI-based drought characterization using a workflow that produces ensemble drought scenarios. Results demonstrate the system’s capacity to facilitate reproducible, portable, and extensible hydrological analyses across a range of spatial and temporal scales. The study discusses the architecture, implementation, and capabilities of the system and explores its implications for collaborative research, education, and low-code scientific computing in hydrology.

title: Coupling agent-based and InVEST® models for spatio-temporal simulation of land-use change effects on ecosystem services
abstract: Understanding complex socio-ecological systems requires integrated spatio-temporal assessment. However, socio-ecological modelling approaches rarely represent both space and time. To address this, we present the simulation framework NetVest which couples existing dynamic simulation models with static models by allowing the dynamic model to control the static one. We applied NetVest to coupling dynamic agent-based models, built in NetLogo, with static models from the InVEST® suite, built in Python. We implemented and tested NetVest in a case study of the effects of smallholder-driven land-use change on economic functions and biodiversity over time and space. This case study demonstrated how examining underlying patterns at different time points deepens understanding of key mechanisms. In conclusion, NetVest enables more realistic modelling of socio-ecological systems by integrating spatial and temporal dynamics. This approach supports the development of more balanced land-use strategies that account for biodiversity conservation and land-use change, marking an important step in socio-ecological research.

title: RiverFlood-1D v 1.0: coupling parabolic and backwater (PAB) scheme and Muskingum-Cunge model for river flood routing, with application to the Po River (Italy)
abstract: RiverFlood-1D is a discharge routing model for simulating flood wave propagation in rivers with arbitrary cross-section geometries. It couples the parabolic-backwater (PAB) scheme with the Muskingum-Cunge (MC) approach, dynamically updating routing parameters at each computational step based on steady water surface profiles that account for downstream conditions. The model was verified against four test cases, including compound channels, mixed flow regimes, and a dam-break experiment with highly irregular cross sections. It was then applied to a real flood event along a 60 km reach of the Po river (Italy, April 2009), achieving mean absolute percentage errors of 0.230 and 0.119 for discharge and water depth, respectively, comparable to HEC-RAS (0.210 and 0.080). RiverFlood-1D remained stable in the dam-break test where HEC-RAS's unsteady solver failed to converge. The model combines accuracy similar to full dynamic-wave solvers with greater numerical robustness, making it well suited for operational, real-time flood-forecasting applications.

title: Bias-corrected exceedance mapping of groundwater nitrate using geostatistical and machine-learning models
abstract: Spatial models used in environmental assessment are often used to predict concentrations, even when the underlying decision problem concerns the delineation of threshold exceedance areas. We show that the common practice of thresholding point predictions can introduce substantial bias in estimated exceedance areas. We propose a decision-aligned modeling and evaluation workflow that frames exceedance mapping as a probabilistic prediction task. The approach calibrates exceedance maps to match an unbiased area estimate and assesses model performance using target-weighted cross-validation. In a groundwater-nitrate case study, several widely used interpolation and machine-learning models underestimate exceedance area by 80%–98% when exceedance areas are derived by thresholding concentration predictions, despite competitive concentration-based error metrics. Area calibration removes this bias and yields a balanced trade-off between omission and commission. The workflow is model-agnostic and compatible with standard geostatistical and machine-learning methods, providing a general framework for task-aligned modeling and uncertainty quantification in environmental applications involving threshold-based decisions.

title: CausalHMoE-STFNN: A two-stage causal-inspired spatio-temporal model for multi-pollutant air quality inference

A physics-informed predictive control framework for joint regulation of water level and velocity in open channels
abstract: Traditional flow regulation in open channel system has focused primarily on maintaining water levels, yet flow velocity is equally critical because it affects sediment transport and aquatic environment. However, accurate integrated control of both water level and velocity variables remains challenging. Although data-driven surrogate models can improve the computational efficiency of hydrodynamic models, their physical interpretability is limited. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics-informed predictive control framework that integrates hydrodynamic principles with data-driven learning for real-time multi-variable regulation. A control-embedded physics-informed neural networks (CEPINNs) is developed to provide fast and physically consistent prediction of hydrodynamic states. Moreover, the CE-PINN is coupled with MPC to establish an efficient, constraint-aware optimization model. This hybrid strategy leverages the rapid prediction capabilities of CE-PINNs and uses HEC-RAS for precise state initialization, ensuring accurate and timely control. The results from numerical case studies demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms traditional data-driven methods in terms of prediction accuracy, particularly in data-scarce scenarios. In the new framework, coordinated tracking of water levels while preventing low-velocity stagnation is achieved, and the online optimization time is significantly reduced compared to using a full hydrodynamic model as the inner predictor. The framework provides insights into the application of smart management in water systems, particularly in open-channel and river engineering.

A potentially transferable grid-based SWAT+ framework for groundwater recharge estimation informed by satellite-derived evapotranspiration in data-scarce volcanic islands
abstract: Quantifying groundwater recharge in data-scarce volcanic islands is essential for sustainable water management, yet challenged by limited monitoring networks and the lack of perennial surface water bodies. This study introduces a potentially transferable grid-based SWAT+ framework, an innovative adaptation of semi-distributed hydrological modeling, to better capture spatiotemporal hydrogeological and climatic heterogeneity in such environments. The framework integrates satellite-derived evapotranspiration for physically consistent parameterization, employing Sobol global sensitivity analysis followed by a two-stage calibration (hydrological ratios and remote sensing-based). Demonstrated on El Hierro (Canary Islands) as a representative case, the model uncovers significant recharge variability influenced predominantly by land use, with secondary controls from soil and topography, yielding mean annual recharge of 58 mm·yr -1 (P05–P95: 31–89 mm·yr -1 ), substantially lower than prior local assessments. By leveraging remote sensing and advanced calibration, this approach enhances accuracy in semi-arid volcanic settings and is potentially applicable to other semi-arid volcanic contexts, enabling resilient water resource planning amid climate change uncertainties.

title: SurtGIS: A high-performance raster geospatial analysis library in Rust with WebAssembly and Python support
A comparative study of deep learning and process-based models for hourly flood simulation under a unified input and optimization framework
EVAonline: An open-source web platform for global reference evapotranspiration estimation via multi-source data fusion
abstract: Accurate modeling of reference evapotranspiration (ET 0 ) is critical for environmental management but is hindered by input uncertainties and data scarcity in emerging agricultural frontiers. We introduce EVAonline, a new open-source, scalable web platform providing robust ET 0 estimation via multi-source data fusion. Built on a modular hexagonal architecture integrating six meteorological APIs, the software implements an adaptive Kalman filter constrained by 30-year climatological priors to harmonize disparate datasets. Validated in Brazil’s MATOPIBA region across 17 sites (186,286 observations), the framework achieved a Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.814. The fusion process significantly mitigated uncertainty, reducing Mean Absolute Error by 50% and systematic bias by 95% compared to individual products. By resolving hydroclimatic modeling challenges in data-scarce regions through software engineering, EVAonline delivers a scalable, open-source decision-support architecture designed for global deployment; its quantitative validation here is restricted to the MATOPIBA region against BR–DWGD, with broader multi-climate and forecast-horizon validation left for future work.

title: A self-supervised deep learning method for retrieving historically similar extreme rainfall patterns
Development of an R package for probabilistic modeling of vapor intrusion based on the Johnson and Ettinger Model
Including rainfall sequencing and autocorrelation adjustment as a component of bias correction for hydroclimate projections
abstract: Bias correction of rainfall data is often required for the production of hydroclimate projections due to the misestimation of important characteristics of the precipitation process in global and/or regional climate models. Most bias correction methods ignore rainfall sequencing and correct the daily distribution only, which can lead to biases in runoff characteristics when corrected rainfall is used as an input into hydrological models. A bias correction method (RhoQM) is developed in which rainfall sequencing is corrected using estimated autocorrelation functions from autoregressive-moving average (ARMA) models. We correct historical and future rainfall from an ensemble of regional climate models for south-eastern Australia and compare the results to standard quantile-quantile mapping. Correctly specifying the autocorrelation function complexity can reduce residual cross-validated bias in rainfall and runoff metrics. There is little difference in future change signal in metrics from different model complexities, which suggests that the method is robust for hydroclimate projections.

title: An interpretable multi-horizon forecasting framework for daily urban CO2 emissions using multisource social sensing data

Ilya M. Sobol’ (1926–2025): The question that shaped global sensitivity analysis
abstract: : The passing of Ilya M. Sobol’ marks the loss of an influential mathematician whose work pioneered and fundamentally shaped global sensitivity analysis (GSA) and modern uncertainty quantification. This tribute reflects on Sobol’s foundational role in GSA, with particular emphasis on the variance-based framework, now widely known as the Sobol’ method . Drawing on historical context and personal recollections from two of his long-time colleagues, it honors Sobol’s scientific and human legacy while considering the continuing importance of sensitivity analysis for understanding increasingly complex and integrated models under uncertainty.

title: Negotiating management alternatives under uncertain future conditions using a self-organizing map framework
abstract: Evaluating the performance of environmental management alternatives requires balancing stakeholder objectives under a wide array of plausible States of the World (SOWs). This paper contributes the MAPS (Mapping Alternative Performance across SOWs) framework, a visual decision-support approach that uses Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), which simultaneously perform clustering and dimension reduction, to help stakeholders compare management alternatives under deep uncertainty. MAPS clusters large ensembles of SOWs into interpretable groups arranged on a two-dimensional map, onto which alternatives’ performance is superimposed. This enables stakeholders to examine how performance varies across conditions, where their goals are met or missed, and how objective tradeoffs are shifted across the plausible space of system conditions. The framework is demonstrated with a Colorado River Basin case study, illustrating how MAPS can identify potential conflict zones between Upper and Lower Basin stakeholders and lead to identification of compromise alternatives.

title: Multiple machine-learning estimation of groundwater levels and trends for the regional Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer
abstract: The Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer provides irrigation, public, and domestic water supplies across the south-central United States. Declining groundwater levels require improved characterization of changing conditions. Traditional potentiometric-surface mapping does not use all available water-level data or quantify uncertainty. To address these limitations, we developed a data-driven multiple machine-learning (MML) framework delivered through two open-source R packages. The covMRVAgen1 software assembles covariates to 155,960 monthly groundwater levels from 57,695 wells; the mmlMRVAgen1 software trains Cubist and Random Forest models, blends them, and makes 1-kilometer gridded predictions of monthly potentiometric surfaces for the period January 1980–December 2022. The MML approach provides a methodological foundation for region-scale spatiotemporal groundwater prediction and uncertainty quantification, generating 90-percent prediction limits with appropriate empirical coverage. Model performance is acceptable, with a root-mean-square error of about 4.2 feet, standard deviation of 24.82 feet, and a normalized Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.973.

title: Editorial Board
Multivariate SWAT streamflow and surface water storage calibration enables upper Mississippi River Basin wetland change scenarios
abstract: Surface water storage (e.g., wetlands, lakes) is not typically considered in hydrological model calibrations. We tested a multivariate calibration process, incorporating Sentinel-1 and -2 surface water storage, for a Soil and Water Assessment Tool model across the 0.5 million km 2 Upper Mississippi River Basin. While 19% of the 2000 parameter sets adequately simulated discharge (Kling-Gupta efficiency >0.5), only 5% also adequately simulated surface water storage (mean absolute error <2 m), reducing model output uncertainty. Using the best calibrated model, we found that changes in surface water storage capacity most strongly affected discharge during the first annual peak flow (i.e., floods), when storage was filling. Increases in upstream surface water storage capacity resulted in projected decreases in peak flow and flashiness, with changes persisting downstream to the watershed outlet. Our findings demonstrate the importance of surface water storage in multivariate model calibration processes to inform river discharge and flood impact predictions.

title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of biochar application as a climate tool in European agriculture: Economic insights
abstract: Biochar application on agricultural land is promoted for its high permanence as a carbon sink. This study examines the spatiotemporal dynamics and economic net benefits of biochar sequestration in EU agricultural soils from 2020 to 2050. A discrete time dynamic economic optimization model, spatially disaggregated across 26 EU member states, evaluates trade-offs between using agricultural residues for biochar, bioenergy, direct soil incorporation, and cover crops. Results show that biochar will become economically viable within the next decade, with optimal carbon stocks reaching 0.6–6.8 tonnes per hectare by 2050. Countries with abundant biomass benefit most due to economies of scale and lower transport costs. By 2050, optimal carbon sequestration yields a net present value of about 212 billion euro, including 36 billion from biochar. Sensitivity analysis underscores the influence of carbon pricing, production costs, and regional biomass supply. Biochar thus offers a cost-effective, regionally variable mitigation option for the EU.

title: Exploring graph neural networks for flood modeling: Challenges, opportunities, and future prospects
abstract: Hydrodynamic flood models play a central role in understanding the spatiotemporal evolution of floods for effective disaster management. Current implementations are limited, as physics-based numerical models are constrained by slow inference times, and data-driven models lack interpretability and physical consistency. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a physically meaningful framework to represent unstructured spatial domains as graphs, mirroring the node–link structure of numerical models. Unlike other deep learning methods, GNNs require no complex spatial data transformation and can seamlessly integrate physics-based priors. This review synthesizes forty nine peer-reviewed studies on GNN applications in flood modeling, identifying key gaps in physics incorporation, scalability, and cross-domain generalization. Drawing on advances from related fields where GNNs have excelled, we outline strategies to overcome these limitations. GNNs hold significant potential as next-generation flood models by combining physical realism, computational efficiency, and adaptability for real-time flood prediction and risk management.

title: Global-RSWQmonitor: Global water quality mapping and monitoring with Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery on Google Earth Engine cloud platform
BiGRU-dXAJ: A hybrid hydrologic model enabling differentiable parameter learning for runoff simulation
Structural investigation of regime-dependent surrogate representations under controlled hydrodynamic conditions: A Mixture-of-Experts approach
abstract: Neural surrogates for environmental systems often struggle with the non-linear, regime-dependent behavior of shallow-water hydrodynamics, such as wetting–drying transitions and floodplain connectivity. This study evaluates a conditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture designed to decompose discharge–inundation mappings into specialized sub-regimes via learned gating.Using 2D hydrodynamic simulations of the Lower Piura River Basin, the MoE surrogate was tested against a single-expert baseline using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Critical Success Index (CSI), and a physics-consistency residual. Results demonstrate that the four-expert MoE significantly improves depth fidelity and volume consistency on unseen hydrographs. Gate trajectories reveal structured specialization aligned with hydrograph phases, while ablation analysis shows that peak performance requires combining conditional gating with explicit inundation-state supervision and physics-informed regularization. These findings suggest that architectural differentiation offers a robust, regime-aware mechanism for representing complex hydrodynamic behaviors, offering a robust framework for investigating regime-aware representations in complex hydrodynamic emulators.

title: Are we eliciting the right preferences? Insights from spatial MCDA sensitivity and uncertainty analysis
Machine learning in urban stormwater management: A review
abstract: Urban stormwater systems generate large and heterogeneous datasets from in-situ sensors, remote sensing, and distributed monitoring networks, yet conventional models often struggle with nonlinear dynamics, data gaps, and scalability. This study presents a structured synthesis of machine learning (ML) approaches for urban stormwater modeling, focusing on their ability to address these limitations. We organize the literature across four domains — water quality prediction, flow modeling, infrastructure management, and real-time control — and introduce an integrated framework linking sensing, prediction, assessment, and adaptive management. Across the reviewed literature, ML provides the greatest value where stormwater applications involve heterogeneous data, nonlinear system behavior, and adaptive decision support; however, reliable deployment remains constrained by both technical and operational barriers including transferability, uncertainty, scalability, and workflow integration. We identify future research needs centered on hybrid physics–ML modeling, benchmark datasets, uncertainty-aware AI, digital twins, and transferable modeling frameworks to support robust and operational stormwater decision-support systems.

Driving analysis of the continuous groundwater decline along the lower Yellow River: Lagged contributions of natural and human factors (2001–2020)
abstract: : The high-sediment perched lower Yellow River forms a distinctive river-aquifer system, with groundwater decline along its banks over the past two decades. Using 2001–2020 data, a framework integrating Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (STL) and an attention-enhanced Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and lag-response was constructed. STL indicated that long-term trends explained 53.12%–91.35% of groundwater-level variance, reflecting a trend-dominated decline. Model applicability varied with spatial and hydrogeological constraints: STL-LSTM resolved periodic near-river seepage (0–5 km; R 2 = 0.888), whereas attention-enhanced LSTM improved predictions in pumped far-river zones (>10 km; R 2 = 0.816). Driver attribution revealed spatial distance-decay in groundwater responses. Near-river groundwater dynamics (0–5 km) were mainly linked to river stage and runoff with an approximately 1-month lag, while high suspended sediment concentration may reduce river-aquifer exchange efficiency. Far-river dynamics (10–15 km) were dominated by agricultural water consumption (maximum contribution: −48.77%).

Stepwise Clustered Ensemble (SCE): An R package for interpretable and robust regression in environmental modeling
abstract: We present Stepwise Clustered Ensemble (SCE), an open-source R package for regression and inference designed to address key limitations of traditional random forest models. SCE replaces impurity splitting with a likelihood-based criterion using Wilks Λ statistic and adds a node-merging step to prevent superfluous partitions. This statistically rigorous construction enhances parsimony and model generalization. The package is fully open-source and designed to integrate seamlessly into reproducible environmental modelling workflows, facilitating transparency and collaboration. The predictors selected by SCE transfer effectively to Random Forest model in the evaluated case studies, improving its performance and offering a practical route to feature selection. Through large-scale environmental applications in hydrology and air-quality modeling, SCE demonstrates strong predictive performance and interpretability while helping reduce overfitting and improve robustness to noisy environmental conditions. By integrating these innovations into an R package, SCE provides researchers with a robust, interpretable, and transferable framework for modeling complex environmental systems.

Large language models for water distribution systems modeling and decision-making
abstract: The design, operations, and management of water distribution systems (WDS) involve complex mathematical models. These models are continually improving due to computational advancements, leading to better decision-making and more efficient WDS management. However, the significant time and effort required for modeling, programming, and analyzing results remain substantial challenges. Another issue is the professional burden, which confines the interaction with models, databases, and other sophisticated tools to a small group of experts, thereby causing non-technical stakeholders to depend on these experts or make decisions without modeling support. Furthermore, explaining model results is challenging even for experts, as it is often unclear which conditions cause the model to reach a certain state or recommend a specific policy. The recent advancements in large language models (LLM) open doors for a new stage in human–model interaction. This study proposes a framework of plain language interactions with hydraulic and water quality models based on LLM-EPANET architecture. This framework is tested with increasing levels of complexity of query to study the ability of LLMs to interact with WDS models, run complex simulations, and report simulation results. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated across several categories of queries and hyperparameter configurations, demonstrating its potential to enhance decision-making processes in WDS management.

Downscaling neural network for coastal simulations
abstract: Learning the fine-scale details of a coastal ocean simulation from a coarse representation is a challenging task. For real-world applications, high-resolution simulations are necessary to advance understanding of many coastal processes, specifically, to predict flooding resulting from tsunamis and storm surges. We propose a Downscaling Neural Network for Coastal Simulation (DNNCS) for spatiotemporal enhancement to learn the high-resolution numerical solution. Given images of coastal simulations produced on low-resolution computational meshes using low polynomial order discontinuous Galerkin discretizations and a coarse temporal resolution, the proposed DNNCS learns to produce high-resolution free surface elevation and velocity visualizations in both time and space. To model the dynamic changes over time and space, we propose grid-aware spatiotemporal attention to project the temporal features to the spatial domain for non-local feature matching. The coordinate information is also utilized via positional encoding. For the final reconstruction, we use the spatiotemporal bilinear operation to interpolate the missing frames and then expand the feature maps to the frequency domain for residual mapping. Besides data-driven losses, the proposed physics-informed loss guarantees gradient consistency and momentum changes, leading to a 24% reduction in root-mean-square error compared to the model trained with only data-driven losses. Our DNNCS is trained on a coastal simulation dataset and uses it for model optimization and evaluation. Our method shows superior downscaling quality and fast computation compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

title: Transforming multimodal data into decision assets: A vision-language model for ecological data using cross-modal alignment
abstract: Environmental monitoring in complex rangeland ecosystems relies on human evaluation to navigate environment shifts. Local community knowledge is important for guiding herd mobility decisions within pastoral systems that use rangeland ecosystems. Currently, human-based scouting considers factors like rangeland location, season, and plant composition to make decisions based on traditional knowledge. However, climate change impact makes rangeland monitoring more complex by reducing the predictability of vegetation availability, species composition, access, and seasonal grazing patterns. To address this, there is a demand to automate rangeland assessment to help sustainable management. We present a novel human-augmented ecological assessment framework that formalizes local community knowledge into a scalable, knowledge-aware AI system through a multimodal Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture with bidirectional cross-attention mechanism. This model is fed by a multimodal dataset from sub-Saharan Africa rangelands collected mainly via a mobile app where stakeholders encode decision-making parameters. This architecture helps the disambiguation of visual features by grounding them in seasonal metadata, which seasonal linguistic guides the model to prioritize site specific phenological patterns over undifferentiated spectral greenness. By employing a MoE layer to manage ecological data variability, our learning model uses community knowledge to override deceptive visual cues and improves rangeland quality classification over unimodal and standard fusion baselines. These results suggest that routing data through human-centric priors can improve rangeland monitoring.

title: SPEIChanges: A framework for assessing climate-change-driven shifts in drought frequency using the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index
abstract: Developing methods based on widely used probability-based indices to quantify how changing climate patterns alter drought occurrence is crucial. In this study, we developed SPEIChanges, an open-source framework designed to quantify how shifts in the central tendency and dispersion of the precipitation-atmospheric evaporative demand (P-AED) distribution affect drought likelihood of occurrence. Simulation results indicated that the Bayesian Information Criterion should be used within the algorithm. We assessed SPEIChanges performance using observed data and climate projections representing contrasting global conditions. The results showed that SPEIChanges characterizes shifts in expected P-AED values and changes in drought frequency. The method explicitly identifies whether these shifts are driven by changes in central tendency, dispersion, or both features. Notably, it detects and quantifies in probabilistic terms changes in drought frequency even when the widely used Mann-Kendall test fails to detect significant trends.

title: UrbanFloodBench: Bridging AI and hydrology through benchmarking of coupled 1D–2D urban flood surrogate models
abstract: Physics-based hydrodynamic models are the standard approach for urban flood simulation but remain computationally prohibitive for real-time forecasting. Although machine learning surrogate models offer a promising alternative, most existing approaches rely on private or simplified datasets, limiting reproducibility and rigorous comparison, particularly for coupled 1D--2D flood systems. To address this gap, we introduce \textit{UrbanFloodBench}, the first open benchmark for coupled 1D--2D urban flood surrogate modelling. UrbanFloodBench combines a multi-catchment dataset, a variance-aware evaluation framework, and a reproducible large-scale AI Kaggle challenge. The benchmark involves 264 teams and 3,799 submissions, producing the first large-scale empirical comparison of AI methods for coupled urban flood emulation. Results show that multiple modelling approaches can achieve strong performance, while the 1D drainage component remains the primary unresolved challenge. UrbanFloodBench establishes a reproducible foundation for advancing AI-based surrogate modelling for urban flood prediction and enabling consistent future evaluation of data-driven flood forecasting methodologies.

title: An effective constraints handling method for medium- to long-term scheduling of water transfer projects under various hydrological scenarios
Integrating MODIS and SMAP data for spatially calibrated SWAT+ modeling in a forested watershed of South Korea
abstract: This study establishes a spatially, multi-variable calibrated SWAT+ methodology integrating Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) leaf area index (LAI) and evapotranspiration (ET) with Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture for the Yongdam Dam watershed, South Korea. Satellite datasets were aggregated by landscape units for parameter calibration and validation. The model reproduced spatial patterns of satellite observations (R 2 > 0.94 for LAI, 0.80 for ET, 0.65 for soil moisture). While utilizing satellite products involves inherent data uncertainties, their integration significantly enhances the physical realism of the SWAT+. The satellite constrained calibration improved the representation of hydrograph dynamics more accurately than conventional calibration. Spatial calibration increased ET (+3.4%) and surface runoff (+1.8%) and decreased groundwater flow (−0.8%), revealing improved representation of surface water processes and energy–water interactions. The methodology demonstrates the utility of remote sensing integration in SWAT+ to enhance spatial realism and reduce parameter equifinality.

KarstNSim 2.0: A pseudo-genetic method for comprehensive karst network simulation
abstract: In this paper, we present KarstNSim 2.0, an upgraded version of the pseudo-genetic method and software KarstNSim for stochastic simulation of discrete karst networks in 3D. Leveraging recently acquired data and new karstogenetic studies on the Barrois Plateau in Meuse (France), our updated method now includes features to account for ghost-rock karstogenesis and model maze patterns with loops in the karst network topology. KarstNSim 2.0 also proposes to simulate the dimensions of conduits by incorporating karstology-driven spatial trends, ghost-rock influence and residual noise. KarstNSim 2.0 is demonstrated on the Barrois Plateau in Meuse, a large region with a complex history of polyphasic karstification, spanning over multiple spatio-temporal phases, each with their specific boundary conditions and karst morphologies. The realization consistency is ensured by a morphological comparison with real networks.

Explainable AI as a diagnostic tool for analyzing spatiotemporal variability in simulated groundwater recharge: Application to a semi-arid river basin
abstract: Groundwater recharge is a vital component for water budget and water availability assessments but is challenging to measure due to its complex dynamics and subsurface occurrence. Process-based modeling tools are often used to simulate recharge. Analyzing the numerous, interacting factors that control recharge is time consuming and computationally expensive. In this study, we develop machine learning (ML) models that predict recharge and use explainable AI (XAI) as a diagnostic tool to understand the drivers of groundwater recharge, capture critical threshold values, and identify high recharge zones. ML models are trained and tested using calibrated SWAT+ simulated recharge values as the response variable. Two ML models are developed: (i) a surrogate model that captures the physics from the SWAT+ simulator by utilizing selected model inputs with a directly comparable definition of distributed parameter values; and (ii) a stand-alone predictor that utilizes commonly available open-source data to predict recharge and has annual temporal and 500 m spatial resolution for the period of 2002 – 2015. The study is implemented in the semi-arid Lower Arkansas river basin in Colorado, USA which contains an alluvial aquifer that is used for agricultural irrigation. Both the surrogate and stand-alone models demonstrated high predictive accuracy with NSE values of 0.98 and 0.91, respectively, when evaluated against test data. Explainable AI assessments show that the simulated groundwater recharge increases significantly when precipitation exceeds approximately 500 mm/year. Irrigation return flow is also identified as a major source of recharge where cultivated land cover is dominant. Unlike the surrogate model, which correctly identifies key drivers of recharge (e.g., precipitation, snow melt), XAI results from the stand-alone model identify some predictor variables that are correlated with simulated recharge (e.g., high slope and certain LULC classes) but don’t physically drive recharge. These results highlight the effectiveness of ML surrogate models to meaningfully analyze physics-based simulation results. Stand-alone ML models may have high predictive accuracy but limited explanatory power in part due to the limited number of physically informative predictor variables that the model is trained on. The methods adopted in this study provide a valuable approach for investigating recharge dynamics in unconfined aquifers.

Integrated economic and environmental modeling of forest biomass for renewable energy in California: Statewide system implementation and application
abstract: Planning forest biomass-to-energy systems requires integrating spatial resource data, supply chain logistics, technoeconomic modeling, and environmental assessment across heterogeneous landscapes. Existing tools typically address these components in isolation, limiting their ability to capture the coupled dynamics that determine project feasibility. This paper presents Forest Resources Renewable Energy Decision Support System (FRREDSS) 2.0, which extends a previously demonstrated web-based decision support software with substantial new computational methods, unifying six interlinked models to evaluate forest biomass energy pathways across California. The system implements an expanding-radius spatial search with cost-optimized greedy selection to solve annual feedstock procurement problems over 20-year planning horizons, aggregating statewide biomass data into 2.1 million harvest clusters characterized by biomass availability, terrain attributes, and road access. A case study of a 25 MW facility in Butte County shows delivered feedstock costs rising from $42.50 to $133.35/BDT over the facility lifetime, with a levelized cost of electricity of $142.72/MWh.

ParetoPick-R: An interactive tool for boosting the interpretability of multi-objective optimisation outputs
abstract: This study presents ParetoPick-R, an R Shiny application for post-processing multi-objective optimisation (MOO) results in environmental modelling. Although MOO is widely used in environmental management, its multi-dimensional and abstract outputs are often hard to interpret and apply directly. ParetoPick-R addresses this challenge by enhancing the interpretability and usability of MOO results for decision support. The tool integrates three key strategies. First, interactive visualisation techniques enable users to explore synergies and trade-offs among objectives and link objective and decision spaces. Second, a clustering-based data reduction approach condenses large Pareto sets into representative subsets while preserving essential trade-off structures. Third, an Analytical Hierarchy Process facilitates the systematic incorporation of stakeholder preferences across objectives and decision variables. This paper describes the design and implementation of ParetoPick-R and demonstrates its functionality and procedural application through two distinct case studies.
